newsitem.title: HONG KONG: WEEK AHEAD - U.S. seen dictating Asian stock moves.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - U.S. seen dictating Asian stock moves.

text.p: Concerns about a U.S. interest rate rise will rule Asian stock markets in the coming week, following sharp moves by the Dow Industrials on economic data last week, traders said.

New York stocks jumped 57 points to 6,935.46 on Friday after sliding 160 points to 6,878.89 on Thursday. A subdued U.S. wholesale price report on Friday helped to settle inflationary fears roused by a stronger than expected retail sales figure for February on Thursday.

Asian stocks responded nervously, with Hong Kong shedding 180.56 points or 1.4 percent to end at 12,736.53 on Friday. Dealers said some markets can expect to gain on the back of Friday's U.S. recovery, but others will continue to suffer from a general outflow of institutional money from Asia.

"There's been net outflows of cash from Asia, and that money seems to be going to more attractive markets," said one head trader. "Taiwan's the only place with an earnings story but it's a local market."
Beneficiaries from the Asian outflow continue to be Latin America and Eastern Europe, he said.
TOKYO - Japanese stocks are likely to see limited upside this coming week, with the market remaining wary of an uncertain economic outlook for the start of a new financial year in April.
Market participants are also waiting to see if there will be any government measures to boost real estate liquidity, which would help prop up Japan's sluggish economy.
On Friday, the Nikkei 225 average finished at 17,923.64, down 275.1 points, or 1.51 percent, from its closing on March 7.
"We are anxious to see if the market can head up after the SQ," said Kenji Karikomi, a deputy general manager at Daiwa Securities Co Ltd.
Brokers said they would pay close attention to government policies to support the real estate market.
"Positive and negative aspects of the outlook for government policies have been mixed so far, but worries are slightly stronger now," said Akihiro Naemura, a strategist at Okasan Securities Co Ltd.
"Until some policies are unveiled, bank and construction shares cannot perk up," said a second-tier brokerage analyst.
HONG KONG - Gains for Hong Kong stocks may be capped in the coming week with many investors on the sidelines awaiting corporate earnings results, analysts and brokers said.
"Sentiment will continue to be cautious in the coming week, although we could see a rebound at the beginning of the week," said Edward Chan, head of research at Amsteel Securities.

The Hang Seng Index plunged more than 280 points on Friday before recovering to end 180 points lower at 12,736.53. Turnover was a frothy HK$12.52 billion. Over the week, the index lost a total of 600.82 points, or 4.50 pct. Turnover averaged HK$12.23 billion a day.
"Interest rate worries are a bit overdone, but many investors may stay on the sidelines until the end of the month," added Chan.
TAIPEI - Taiwan share prices were expected to inch cautiously higher next week after reaching a fresh six-year high on Saturday, brokers said.
Taiwan's index soared to 8,291.31, up 108.87 points or 1.33 percent against last Saturday's close of 8,182.44.
Strong buying in electronics shares was behind the rally, but brokers warned the index was quickly approaching resistance at 8,450 points.
"Sentiment will be cautious next week," said George Hou, a fund manager at Jardine Fleming.
A hotly-contested county by-election and the upcoming visit by Tibet's exiled spiritual leader, the Dalai Lama, could weigh on sentiment in the coming week, brokers said.

The Dalai Lama's planned six-day visit to Taiwan beginning on March 22 is likely to draw angry protests from Beijing, which maintains that Taiwan's leaders and the exiled Tibetan god-king seek Taiwan's and Tibet's independence from China.
"People will step back a bit next week in the wake of the two uncertain factors, but the market should find strong support at the 8,000-point level," said Eric Liu, analyst for National Securities.

BANGKOK - The Stock Exchange of Thailand (SET) index is expected to retreat slightly next week on worries about the future success of Thailand's first batch of zero-coupon bonds, aimed at helping out the country's beleaguered property sector.

"Some investors are starting to ask questions whether the scheme would function smoothly when it starts operating. These investors are likely to sell next week," said Kasem Prunratanamala, analyst at James Capel Asia.
The first tranche of the 100 billion baht zero-coupon bonds is expected in April.
Brokers said Thai investors, already under pressure from high domestic rates, would also be cautious ahead of the March 25 meeting of the U.S. Federal Open Market Committee.
"Investors are a bit worried that the U.S. Fed would raise its interest rates because any increase would affect the rates in Thailand," said Kasem.
The SET index rose 0.5 percent in the week to 694.91 points on Friday from a week ago.
JAKARTA - Jakarta share prices are expected to be mixed next week but trading would be relatively slow amid concerns of a possible U.S. interest rate hike, brokers said.
Possible further bargain-hunting in banking stocks and the expected announcement of 1996 corporate results could boost the overall market sentiment, they said.
On Friday, the Jakarta Composite Index closed 3.15 points lower at 666.84 points on Friday, against the previous week's close of 683.81 points.
KUALA LUMPUR - Malaysian shares are likely to extend their consolidation into next week although bargain hunting in selected stocks may limit losses, dealers said.

"It will be a bit volatile next week with direction of the Dow still very much uncertain," said one institutional dealer with a local firm. He said fears of a U.S. interest rate hike would continue to limit participation from funds.
Dealers said with institutions likely to keep to the sidelines, the market would continue to focus on retail interest in small-capitalised second board stocks.
For the week, the benchmark Composite Index of 100 large-capitalised stocks closed down 8.74 points to 1,242.47 against 1,251.21 the previous week.
MANILA - Wall Street's interest rate jitters will dictate the direction of Manila shares next week, traders said.

"We will essentially be a slave to the performance of the Dow which would in turn depend on how big the fear is of an interest rate hike in the U.S.," said Felix Barrientos, dealer at ING Baring Securities (Phils) Inc.
Traders said if the Dow dips further, it may be a signal that foreign funds are moving back to the region. Otherwise, trading will still centre on second and thirdliners.
The main index closed at 3,234.79 points on Friday, 51.66 points, or 1.57 percent lower than the previous week's 3,286.45.
SINGAPORE - Singapore shares were likely to slip further over the coming week with blue chip companies expected to continue disappointing the market with lacklustre results, dealers said.
"In the short term, there's not a lot of good news to lift the market," said a dealer with a local firm.
First quarter domestic export figures due next week were unlikely to show the hoped-for economic recovery to be in full swing, brokers said.
The benchmark Straits Times Industrial index ended at 2,135.46 Friday -- a new low for 1997 -- down 42.81 points over last week's close.
SEOUL - Seoul shares could see a brief technical rebound next week, but the mid-term outlook for the market remained poor, brokers said.
"The economic environment is full of bad news, making it hard for the KOSPI to maintain any uptrend," said Kevin Choi, a fund manager at Seoul Investment Trust Co.
Poor fundamentals include high interest rates, a faltering won, fears of tightening liquidity and a slowing economy.
The Seoul index closed at 641.83 on Saturday, 33.24 points or 4.9 percent weaker than last Saturday's close of 675.07.
SYDNEY - Australian shares were seen nervous in the near-term with attention now firmly focused on Wall Street.

The All Ordinaries index closed down 1.2 percent on Friday at 2,423.2, and down 0.6 percent over the week. All eyes were on U.S. markets as traders waited to see if U.S. interest rate fears would abate.
"If sentiment does remain negative in the short term, then you may see a bit of an overreaction on the downside before the market stabilises," said Derek Bond, director at brokerage Burrell and Co.
WELLINGTON - New Zealand shares tumbled on heavy volume on Friday as Wall Street's sharp fall unsettled an already fragile market.
John Rattray of brokers Ord Minnett said international investors were currently net sellers of New Zealand equities and the outlook was poor.
"I think this market is going through a very awkward stage," he said.
The NZSE-40 capital index closed 24.39 points or 1.08 percent lower on the day at 2,226.60, its lowest finish since October 10. The index has fallen 62.26 points or 2.72 percent in the past week.
BOMBAY - Indian shares are expected to recover next week but buyers will be watching a crucial budget debate in parliament, traders said.
"The market's overbought positions are pretty much squared up," said Ramesh Damani, a member-broker of the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE). "The bull run should now resume."
The minority coalition government faces a tough task piloting a pro-business 1997/98 (April-March) budget presented to parliament on February 28, traders said.
The BSE index lost 130.73 points, or 3.4 percent, to 3,745.31 this week after rallying 16 percent since the budget.

DHAKA - Dhaka stocks suffered heavily before bouncing back in response to a central bank move to offer credit to investors in the capital market and analysts said the market may attract fresh investments.

"We expect fresh commitments from Sunday as the ICB (state-owned institutional brokerage) has raised credit to small investors. The central bank has also asked commercial banks to double bank loans to the investors," said one broker.
The market experienced some recovery on Tuesday and Wednesday and the trend may continue next week. The DSE benchmark index lost 82.88 points to close at 1,523.67 in the week to Thursday.
